en.definition: A controlled comparison in which two versions of a learning experience, interface, message, or intervention are presented to different groups so their effects can be compared.
The xAPI resource at /about that returns basic information about an LRS, including supported xAPI versions and optional extensions.
The practice of designing learning technologies, content, and interactions so people with a wide range of abilities can perceive, operate, understand, and use them.
Testing that checks whether a learning solution can be used by people with different abilities, access needs, contexts, and constraints.
An xAPI identity structure that represents an Agent or Group through an account on an existing system using a home page for the account system and a unique account name.
The foundational AI competency level in which teachers develop the essential knowledge, ethical awareness, and practical skills needed to evaluate, select, and use AI tools appropriately.

In xAPI, an Activity is something an Actor interacts with or experiences and that can serve as the object of a tracked Statement. Activities can represent instruction, performance, experiences, resources, events, or even physical or virtual objects.
The optional metadata object within an xAPI Activity that can describe its human-readable name, description, type, more-information location, interaction details, and extensions.
The xAPI resource at /activities/profile for storing and retrieving generic profile documents associated with an Activity.
The individual or group represented in an xAPI Statement as performing the action described by the Statement.
A hypermedia system that builds a model of the user and changes the information, links, or presentation shown to that user rather than presenting the same experience to everyone.
A learning system that changes content, sequencing, support, feedback, or difficulty in response to evidence about a learner or context.
Data generated through the routine administration and management of an education system, commonly through education management information systems and related government records.
A field of computing concerned with recognizing, modeling, or responding to human emotional states and, in some cases, simulating affective behavior in machines.
The xAPI resource at /agents/profile for storing and retrieving generic profile documents associated with an Agent or Identified Group, independent of a specific Activity or registration.
An iterative approach to creating solutions in small increments, learning from feedback, and adapting plans as conditions change.

en.prefLabel: AI competency framework for teachers (AI CFT)
en.definition: A reference framework describing the knowledge, skills, values, and attitudes teachers need to use artificial intelligence safely, effectively, ethically, and in ways that preserve human-centred education.
A scaffolded reference pathway for developing AI competency across increasing levels of capability without assuming that development is strictly linear or identical across competency areas.
The extent to which educators can understand and critically examine how an AI system reaches outputs or conclusions sufficiently to assess its use and intervene when necessary.
The use of AI to support teachers’ lifelong professional learning, collaborative development, reflection, assessment of learning needs, and transformation of professional practice.
The conceptual knowledge and transferable operational skills needed to understand how AI works and to evaluate, select, use, adapt, or customize AI tools for appropriate purposes.

The foundational set of AI competencies teachers need to understand AI’s human-led nature, recognize benefits and risks, apply core ethical principles, understand basic AI concepts, and use appropriate AI tools in educational practice.
The competencies and practices involved in selecting, validating, and integrating AI with pedagogical methods to support teaching, learning, social interaction, care, and assessment.

The systematic evaluation of an AI system or tool before educational adoption to determine whether it is sufficiently reliable, trustworthy, safe, ethically compliant, age-appropriate, and pedagogically suitable.
Teaching in which educators identify and use appropriate AI tools to support activities such as lesson planning, instruction, assessment, and learner support while mitigating associated risks.

The critical and exploratory use of AI to develop or transform learning scenarios, pedagogical approaches, assessment, and student-centred learning while maintaining human-centred educational principles.

The purposeful integration of AI into student-centred learning design and facilitation to support engagement, differentiated learning, teacher–student interaction, critical thinking, and problem-solving.
An xAPI Group without its own Inverse Functional Identifier, represented through the Agents listed as its members.
A broad class of computational techniques used to perform tasks associated with perception, prediction, classification, generation, decision support, or other forms of intelligent behavior.
The collection and interpretation of evidence about knowledge, skill, performance, learner state, or learning outcomes.
An approach that begins with the capabilities and strengths a learner already possesses and focuses on adding new capabilities rather than primarily diagnosing deficits against group averages.
Learning activity that can occur at different times, allowing learners to engage with materials or tasks without everyone participating simultaneously.
A file or other binary resource logically associated with an xAPI Statement, described by metadata including usage type, display name, content type, length, SHA-2 hash, and optionally a file URL.
The selective allocation of cognitive resources to information, tasks, or stimuli.

Foundational and broad fields of study intended to develop general knowledge, literacies, cultural understanding, and core academic capabilities across areas such as language, mathematics, science, humanities, arts, health, and civic learning.
A field that studies systematic biases, heuristics, and decision patterns that cause people to make choices that depart from purely rational models.
A systematic distortion in data, measurement, analysis, models, processes, or decisions that can produce unfair or misleading results.
The development of increasingly organized, retrievable, and usable knowledge and skill within a domain through experience and practice.
The stage of learning engineering in which a team frames the problem, context, stakeholders, constraints, and evidence before designing a solution.
The period between the end of paid parental leave and the age at which children become legally entitled to access early childhood education and care services.
Professional teaching personnel primarily responsible for planning, organising, and conducting group learning activities that guide students' learning experiences.
A collaborative design approach in which researchers or designers work with practitioners, learners, partners, or other affected participants to shape questions, technologies, and practices.
The degree to which a learner actively thinks about, applies, analyzes, and connects knowledge rather than only receiving or memorizing information.
The mental effort required to process information in working memory during a task.
A family of methods for identifying the knowledge, decisions, cues, strategies, and mental processes involved in performing complex tasks.
A usability inspection method in which evaluators step through a task from the perspective of a user and ask whether each action is understandable and discoverable.
A community in which people learn through social participation in a shared practice, developing knowledge through interaction with others engaged in related work or activity.
A defined capability, skill, knowledge area, or observable performance that can be described, assessed, developed, or referenced across systems.
An approach in which progress is organized around demonstrated mastery of defined competencies rather than primarily around time spent in a course or program.
The use of computers to access training or education through synchronous or asynchronous activities delivered on networked or standalone systems.
A representation that shows how concepts or abstract ideas are connected to one another.
Knowledge of the ideas, relationships, and underlying reasons that explain why a procedure, principle, or solution works.

A learning theory that treats knowledge as distributed across networks of connections and emphasizes continual learning, current information, and the ability to recognize connections among sources and fields.
A massive open online course organized around connectivist principles, emphasizing networks, social learning, cooperation, and collaborative knowledge construction.
Activity references included in an xAPI Statement Context to express how the recorded experience relates to broader or associated Activities.
An xAPI context structure that represents a Statement-specific relationship between the Statement and a relevant Agent, optionally characterized by one or more relationship-type IRIs.
An xAPI context structure that represents a Statement-specific relationship between the Statement and a relevant Group, optionally characterized by one or more relationship-type IRIs.

The optional xAPI Statement component used to add surrounding information about an experience, such as registration, related activities, relevant Agents or Groups, language, platform, another Statement, or extensions.
A condition surrounding a design, such as learner needs, curriculum structure, timeline, resources, or technology, that can influence what is feasible or appropriate.
A learning environment understood and designed in relation to the specific people, practices, technologies, constraints, and settings in which learning occurs.
An ongoing practice of using evidence and feedback to refine learning experiences, systems, processes, and operations over time.
A software development practice in which changes are integrated and tested frequently rather than accumulated into large, infrequent releases.
An engineering field concerned with how systems use feedback to regulate behavior and move toward desired states.
A managed set of defined terms and identifiers used consistently within a domain so that people and machines can refer to the same concepts in the same way.

A sustained network or coordinating structure that connects participants, brokers relationships, supports collaborative work, synthesizes outcomes, and helps knowledge move across projects and communities.

The advanced AI competency level in which teachers critically and creatively configure, adapt, or co-create AI-enabled approaches, tools, policies, and pedagogical practices for educational transformation.

The part of the learning engineering process in which a team creates a response to a learning challenge by designing the solution, planning and instrumenting the needed data, and iterating the design with learners and stakeholders.
Collaboration among people from different professional disciplines who contribute distinct expertise to a learning engineering challenge.
A regional or international learning assessment that uses a common agreed framework and similar procedures across participating systems to produce comparable learning-outcome data.
The deliberate effort to shift shared assumptions, behaviors, norms, incentives, and ways of working so an organization can adopt and sustain a new model of learning.
The planned subjects and learning content of an educational program, including how instructional time is allocated and how learning is sequenced.
The interpretation of data to derive insights, identify trends, evaluate outcomes, diagnose drivers, and assess policy effects.
The use of methods and tools to examine data in order to describe patterns, test hypotheses, identify relationships, or support decisions.
The condition in which data exists and can be accessed or retrieved, regardless of whether it has been officially reported or whether its quality is sufficient for a particular use.
An organizational and institutional environment in which transparency, collaboration, participation, openness, shared definitions, and the regular use of evidence support decision-making.
The deliberate design and implementation of mechanisms that capture events, states, context, and other data needed to understand a learning system.
The use of computational methods to discover patterns, structures, associations, or predictive relationships in large datasets.
The rights, responsibilities, and governance questions associated with control over data generated or used within education systems.
A sequence of processes that moves, validates, transforms, enriches, stores, or routes data from source systems to destinations.
The principles and practices that govern how information about people is collected, used, shared, retained, protected, and deleted.
The degree to which data is accurate, complete, consistent, timely, valid, and fit for its intended use.
The official sharing of available data with the public, international organizations, or other stakeholders.
The practices and controls used to protect learning data, systems, interfaces, storage, and communications from unauthorized access, manipulation, loss, or disruption.
An isolated store of data that does not readily exchange information with other applications, systems, or organizational data sources.
The organizational responsibility for governing how data is held, protected, accessed, shared, maintained, and used across its lifecycle.
The application of data and analytical findings to policy and programme development, resource allocation, planning, implementation, and other decisions intended to improve education.
A decision process that uses relevant data as evidence while also considering context, expertise, goals, and constraints.
The use of data, analytics, models, or software to help people make informed decisions without necessarily automating the decision itself.
The practice of recording design decisions, their justifications, sources of influence, and revisions across the life of a design project.

The intermediate AI competency level in which teachers integrate AI into educational practice with greater attention to human accountability, safe and responsible use, ethical evaluation, and pedagogical design.
A choice about what to include in a learning design and how that choice will be enacted, made in response to goals, evidence, experience, constraints, and context.
The process of forming, enacting, communicating, revisiting, and sometimes revising choices about a learning design while accounting for learners, stakeholders, evidence, technology, and context.
The reasoning used to determine why a design choice is appropriate in a particular situation, drawing on knowledge, experience, theory, and contextual factors.
The recorded reason, evidence, or source of influence that explains why a design decision was made or revised.
A reusable description of a recurring design problem and a proven or commonly useful way of addressing it.
A change to something previously decided or to an existing element of a learning design.

An iterative cycle in which a learning solution is designed, built, tried with learners or stakeholders, examined through evidence, and revised rather than treated as complete after a single design pass.
A digitally represented claim about achievement, qualification, skill, identity, participation, or authorization that can be issued and verified electronically.
Inequality in access to technology infrastructure and in the skills needed to benefit from digital technologies.
The application of digital engineering methods, models, interfaces, and lifecycle thinking to the design and operation of learning systems.
Data produced through the use of technology in teaching and learning that can be collected, analyzed, and shared.

Reusable digital resources intended for broad public benefit, including research, digital resources and applications, databases, repositories, standards, algorithms, and platforms that can be adapted across contexts.
Digital content and resources used to support teaching and learning, including digital textbooks, simulations, games, user-created content, and open educational resources.
The capabilities needed to benefit from digital technologies and to use them effectively in learning and teaching, including the use of digital pedagogies rather than technology use alone.
The protection of digital systems and education data from risks that can undermine confidentiality, integrity, availability, or safe use.
Skills for using digital technologies, ranging from basic technology competencies to higher-order capabilities such as coding, computational thinking, and ethics.

Learning delivered beyond a single physical classroom through distributed technologies and environments, including distance education, online learning, simulations, mobile learning, and other network-enabled experiences.
Simulation conducted across networked systems so multiple participants or simulated entities can interact within a shared scenario or synthetic environment.
An xAPI construct for storing document-style information about an Agent or Activity in name-and-document pairs meaningful to an instructional system component. It is distinct from an xAPI Profile.

The educational component of early childhood education and care, comprising ISCED level 0 programmes with organised and intentional learning activities that support children's cognitive, physical, social, and emotional development.

Services and programmes that support the education, development, well-being, and care of young children before primary education, including ISCED level 0 programmes and regulated childcare outside the formal education system.
The network of public, private, academic, civil-society, donor, school, family, and learner stakeholders involved in developing, providing, governing, and using education technology.
The process through which people develop abilities, attitudes, knowledge, and forms of behavior that are valued within the society in which they live.
A recurring sequence in which education data is produced and made available, reported and shared, analyzed, and then used to inform decisions and further data needs.
The interconnected set of data sources, production and reporting processes, analytical practices, institutions, and uses that together support evidence-based decision-making in an education system.
The combination and linkage of data from different education and related sources to create a more coherent view, fill information gaps, and support analysis that a single source cannot provide.
Financial data describing income and spending related to education from public, private, household, and other sources, including spending on infrastructure, personnel, and other education costs.
An information system used by education authorities to collect, process, analyze, monitor, and disseminate administrative data for education management and planning.
The capability of an education system to produce, report, assess, and use education data of sufficient coverage and quality to generate indicators and support policy and governance.
The use of hardware, software, digital content, data, and information systems in education to support teaching, learning, education management, and delivery.
The organization and administration of part or all of an education system, including the structures and processes used to coordinate, regulate, supervise, and support educational activity.
The highest level of education that an individual has successfully completed.
The systematic assessment of educational performance or quality, including evaluation of learners, teachers, curricula, prior learning, institutions, and educational outcomes.
The physical and material resources that support education, including buildings, equipment, learning resources, playgrounds, and other academic or school facilities.
An entity whose sole or principal purpose is to provide instructional services, or related clinical, community, or research services.

Organizations and establishments that provide education, including schools, higher education institutions, training centers, adult education institutions, and other settings in which organized learning takes place.
The management of educational establishments, including the academic, operational, staffing, resource, attendance, financial, and organizational activities needed to run them.
The systematic process of analyzing educational needs, setting goals and priorities, anticipating future requirements, and organizing resources and actions to improve an education system.
The goals, principles, and official directions that guide an education system and shape decisions about access, rights, priorities, standards, resources, and reform.
The people who participate in and support education systems, including learners, teachers, administrators, advisers, planners, support staff, and other educational personnel.

The interdisciplinary study of education and the environments in which teaching and learning occur, including pedagogical, psychological, social, historical, philosophical, cultural, and contextual influences.
The organized structures through which formal and nonformal education is provided, including the institutions, programs, pathways, and successive stages or levels that make up an education system.
Effects, uses, outcomes, or extensions of exploratory work that develop beyond what was specified or anticipated at the start of a project.
The effort to understand users’ needs, experiences, constraints, motivations, and contexts from their point of view.
A structured technique for organizing observations about what users say, do, think, feel, need, or experience.
An entry point used for communication with a service. In xAPI, resource locations are exposed through IRIs or URLs rooted at an LRS endpoint.
A problem-solving process that develops and evaluates solutions against requirements, evidence, constraints, interfaces, and tradeoffs.
An organizational record that integrates learner-related data across experiences, systems, programs, or time.

Co-design that deliberately lowers barriers to participation, includes underrepresented perspectives, accounts for intersecting identities and needs, and gives practitioners or users meaningful influence over design decisions.
The consideration of whether learning opportunities, technologies, processes, and outcomes fairly account for different needs and conditions.
An approach in which ethical requirements are intentionally built into the design and validation of AI systems rather than addressed only after deployment.
The body of ethical values, principles, regulations, institutional rules, and practical guidance used to evaluate and govern the design and use of artificial intelligence.
The use of data and evidence to inform decisions about teaching, learning, programs, policy, and the management of education systems.
The use of credible research and empirical evidence to inform the design, implementation, and refinement of learning experiences and systems.
A design practice focused on shaping the sensory, emotional, cognitive, behavioral, and social qualities of an experience so it becomes more meaningful and memorable.
Learning in which knowledge is created through experience and reflection, often described as a recursive process of experiencing, reflecting, thinking, and acting.
Research organized to investigate open questions, emerging possibilities, and uncertain design spaces where questions, methods, or outcomes may evolve as evidence is gathered.
A large-scale open online course model that retains open access and scale while generally using more traditional instructivist course structures.
A concrete artifact, such as a sketch, model, concept map, or prototype, that makes design thinking visible so it can support reflection, communication, collaboration, and iteration.
Mental effort caused by features of a task or presentation that do not directly support the learning goal.
The evaluation of whether data, models, assessments, processes, or decisions treat people and groups appropriately under relevant criteria.
A cycle in which information about outcomes or system behavior is returned to learners, instructors, designers, or systems and used to influence subsequent action.
An instructional approach that moves direct content delivery outside class time and uses shared face-to-face time for more interactive learning activities.
A state of deep engagement in which challenge and skill are well matched and attention is strongly focused on the activity.
Assessment used during learning to generate information that can guide improvement, feedback, instruction, or next steps rather than only certify a final outcome.
Evaluation primarily intended to provide feedback that can be used to improve teaching, management, implementation, or school effectiveness.
A standardised measure of teacher workload relative to full-time employment, expressed against the normal statutory working hours for the reference period.
A teacher who has satisfied all training and administrative requirements for teaching a specified grade and subject under a country's formal policy.

A vision of learning as a connected, lifelong continuum rather than a series of disconnected episodes, with experiences tailored to individuals across locations, media, organizations, and periods of time.
The belief that abilities can develop through effort, effective strategies, feedback, and learning over time.
The principle that people remain responsible for decisions and outcomes in human–AI decision loops and that accountability should not be transferred to an AI system.
The capacity of people to retain meaningful autonomy, judgement, and control when evaluating and using AI systems rather than allowing AI to displace human decision-making.
The people, roles, practices, and organizational structures that provide guidance, coaching, instruction, facilitation, or other support to learners.
An approach to education that treats learning as a socially intensive human endeavor and uses technology to support relationships among learners, educators, and communities.
An approach to AI that places human capacities, rights, inclusion, safety, accountability, and sustainable development at the centre of the design, selection, use, and monitoring of AI systems.
A values- and attitudes-based orientation toward human–AI interaction that keeps human rights, human flourishing, human agency, and human accountability central to the use of AI.
The principle that the selection, use, monitoring, and consequential decisions involving AI remain under meaningful human control and human accountability.
A philosophy and set of processes for addressing human performance at the system level throughout design, development, operation, and the broader system lifecycle.
An xAPI Group that has its own Inverse Functional Identifier, allowing the Group to be recognized independently of its current member list.

en.prefLabel: IEEE 1484.11.1-2022 — Data Model for Content Object Communication
en.definition: An IEEE standard defining the data model used to exchange learner, interaction, objective, status, timing, preference, and score information between a learning content object and a runtime service, typically within an LMS environment.

en.prefLabel: IEEE 1484.11.2-2020 — ECMAScript API for Content-to-Runtime Communication
en.definition: An IEEE standard defining an ECMAScript application programming interface for communication between learning content and a runtime service, typically supplied by a Learning Management System. It standardizes common API services used to exchange runtime learning data.

An IEEE standard defining the conceptual data schema for metadata that describes learning objects, including characteristics such as lifecycle, educational use, technical requirements, rights, relationships, annotations, and classifications.

en.prefLabel: IEEE 1484.12.3-2020 — XML Binding for Learning Object Metadata
en.definition: An IEEE standard defining a W3C XML Schema binding for the Learning Object Metadata (LOM) data model so LOM metadata instances can be encoded in XML and exchanged consistently between systems.

en.prefLabel: IEEE 1484.13.3-2014 — MPEG-21 Digital Item Declaration Mapping
en.definition: An IEEE recommended practice mapping elements and attributes from the MPEG-21 Digital Item Declaration model to the IEEE conceptual model for aggregating learning, education, and training resources.

An IEEE recommended practice mapping the elements and attributes of IMS Content Packaging Information Model Version 1.2 to the IEEE conceptual model for resource aggregation used in learning, education, and training.

An IEEE recommended practice mapping the Open Archives Initiative Object Reuse and Exchange (OAI-ORE) Abstract Model and its RDF/XML resource-map representation to the IEEE conceptual model for resource aggregation.

en.prefLabel: IEEE 1484.2-2024 — Learning and Employment Record Ecosystems
en.definition: An IEEE recommended practice for ecosystem-scale systems that issue, hold, present, and exchange Learning and Employment Records (LERs) representing education, skills, employment, and related achievements using interoperable digital credentials and shared services.

An IEEE recommended practice for defining competencies and competency frameworks, including the information needed to describe skills, knowledge, abilities, attitudes, habits of practice, behaviors, and learning outcomes in ways that can support interoperable data.

An IEEE standard defining a data model for describing, referencing, and sharing competency definitions, competency frameworks, and rubrics across learning, credentialing, workforce, and employment systems.

en.prefLabel: IEEE 1589-2020 — Augmented Reality Learning Experience Model
en.definition: An IEEE standard for interoperable augmented-reality learning systems. It defines a conceptual model for relationships among the physical world, the learner, digital information, learning activities, and the environment, along with data models and XML/JSON bindings for representing activities and context.

An IEEE learning technology standard that defines an extensible set of metadata classes and properties for describing learning resources and learning events. Its model is designed to align with Resource Description Framework (RDF) approaches and can be represented in graph-oriented and other formats.

en.prefLabel: IEEE 2955-2025 — Self-Learning Tutorials and Side-by-Side Learning
en.definition: An IEEE recommended practice describing methods for creating self-learning tutorials, including screencast-based and spoken tutorials, with guidance for side-by-side learning techniques.

An IEEE standard defining a framework for digital intelligence, including digital literacy, skills, and readiness. The framework spans eight areas of digital life — identity, use, safety, security, emotional intelligence, literacy, communication, and rights — across citizenship, creativity, and competitiveness levels.

The IEEE standard for the xAPI data model and RESTful web service used to communicate learner and human-performance experience data between activities and a Learning Record Store (LRS). It standardizes the JSON-based model and service behavior derived from xAPI 1.0.3.
An IEEE standards committee that develops and maintains standards for learning technology and related data interoperability.
The stage in which a learning solution is deployed into its intended environment, monitored, supported, and adjusted based on evidence.
The use of models to infer latent states, relationships, or explanations from observed data.
A professional who analyzes learning needs and designs, develops, implements, and evaluates instruction, learning experiences, and supporting materials or systems.
Learning in which an instructor actively guides, structures, supports, or responds to learners as they engage with learning activities.
The sensors, software, schemas, event definitions, identifiers, and processes used to observe and record what happens in a system.
A computer-based instructional system that uses automated procedures to guide learners through problems, provide hints, deliver feedback, and adapt support based on learner performance.
An xAPI Activity Definition used to describe an interaction such as true-false, choice, fill-in, matching, performance, sequencing, Likert, numeric, or other response formats.
Exploratory research that brings together expertise, methods, and perspectives from multiple disciplines to investigate emerging questions and develop novel approaches.

A professional identity in which researchers understand their work as belonging across disciplinary boundaries and participate in collaborations, methods, and communities that span established fields.

A globally unique identifier format used throughout xAPI to identify things such as Verbs, Activities, Activity types, extensions, and other vocabulary concepts. IRIs can contain international characters and include a scheme.
In the xAPI standard, an IRL is an IRI that can be translated to a URI that functions as a URL.
An identifier used by xAPI to uniquely identify a particular Agent persona or Group, such as a mailbox, mailbox hash, OpenID, or account.
The part of the learning engineering process in which collected data are analyzed to explore outcomes and determine how well a solution addresses the learning challenge.
A design approach in which solutions are repeatedly created, tested, evaluated, and refined.
A lightweight text format for representing structured data using objects, arrays, names, and values.
A JSON-based linked-data format that maps familiar JSON structures to semantic identifiers and relationships that can be interpreted as RDF.
A workflow management method that visualizes work, limits work in progress, and supports continuous flow.
The persistence of learned knowledge or skill over time so that it can be retrieved and used later.
An xAPI dictionary whose keys are RFC 5646 language tags and whose values are strings in the corresponding languages.

A UNESCO Institute for Statistics assessment framework for evaluating and strengthening national education data ecosystems across learning assessments, administrative data, survey systems, expenditure data, and review and monitoring.
A family of approaches that combine iterative development with attention to flow, waste reduction, rapid feedback, and value delivery.
The capacity and opportunity for learners to make choices, exercise control, and take an active role in directing aspects of their own learning.
A feedback cycle in which evidence about learner activity or outcomes informs subsequent guidance, practice, support, or system behavior.
A representation of a learner's relevant characteristics, such as knowledge, skills, performance, preferences, goals, context, or other states used to inform instruction or personalization.
The protection and management of privacy interests associated with the collection, modeling, sharing, storage, and use of data about learners and their activities.
Differences among learners in needs, backgrounds, abilities, contexts, experiences, and ways of engaging with or using a learning system.
The analysis and use of data from learning environments to understand and improve learning experiences, instructional strategies, and related decisions.
A visual interface that presents learning analytics, activity patterns, performance indicators, relationships, or recommended interventions for learners and other stakeholders.
A structured process for measuring learners’ knowledge and skills in specified subject areas at particular ages or grade levels, often to estimate learning outcomes for a wider education system.
A group of learners who work together on problems or learning goals within physical or virtual spaces supported by shared norms, processes, and scaffolds.
An umbrella term for practitioners who design learning resources or experiences, including roles such as instructional designer, learning engineer, and learning technologist.
The structures and processes used to coordinate authorities, policies, resources, standards, support, experimentation, and decision making across a learning ecosystem.
A professional who applies evidence about human learning and development at scale to create reliable, affordable, data-rich learning environments within real contexts.

en.prefLabel: Learning Engineering Evidence and Decision (LEED) tracker
en.definition: A learning-engineering documentation structure for recording design decisions, related justifications, sources of influence, and revisions in connection with the learning engineering process.
The person or interdisciplinary group assembled to address a learning challenge, with the mix of skills and knowledge determined by the problem, context, learners, stakeholders, and technical needs.
The combined physical, digital, social, organizational, and instructional conditions in which learning occurs.
The application of engineering and systems methods to the design, integration, and improvement of learning environments.
A discrete occurrence or interaction that can be observed or recorded as part of a learning or performance experience.
An event associated with learning, broadly interpreted to include formal and informal experiences such as courses, reading, field experiences, self-directed work, or receiving a certificate.
The design of experiences, environments, interactions, and supports intended to help people learn.
Structured descriptive information about learning resources, activities, competencies, or related entities.
A network of relationships among learners, teachers, parents, and wider communities that supports teaching and learning across institutional boundaries.
An organization that develops the capacity to learn from evidence and experimentation, test iterative solutions, and adjust practice based on what is learned.
A measure of the share of 10-year-old children who cannot read and understand a simple story.
An xAPI Client that retrieves Learning Records from one or more Learning Record Stores for processing such as interpretation, analysis, translation, dissemination, or aggregation.
Software or a system component that observes activity and sends standards-based learning event records to a Learning Record Store.
A view of learning as continuous across the full lifespan and across formal, nonformal, informal, workplace, community, and lived experiences.
A way of publishing and connecting structured data on the Web using persistent identifiers and machine-readable relationships so information can be linked across datasets and systems.
A belief about whether outcomes are primarily influenced by one's own actions or by forces outside one's control.
The system of memory that supports durable storage and later retrieval of knowledge and skills over extended periods.
Computational methods that learn patterns from data in order to make predictions, classifications, recommendations, or other outputs.
An online course designed for open access and participation at large scale, often serving learners across institutions and geographic boundaries.
An instructional approach that expects learners to demonstrate a defined level of proficiency before moving on to more advanced material or competencies.
A staged framework used to assess current capability and guide incremental improvement over time rather than treating compliance with the highest level as the sole objective.
Learning characterized by intentional, active, constructive, authentic, and cooperative engagement that helps learners connect experiences and build usable understanding.
A developmental relationship in which a more experienced person models knowledge or skills and gives a learner progressively more complex opportunities to participate in authentic work.
Adaptation across multiple learning systems or resources, where one system can use shared data to recommend or coordinate interventions beyond its own immediate instructional environment.
A learner’s awareness and regulation of their own thinking, understanding, strategies, and learning processes.
The process of observing and judging one's own understanding, performance, strategies, and progress while learning or performing a task.
A person, organization, software program, or other entity that determines the meaning represented by an IRI or retrieves metadata about that IRI.
A person, organization, software program, or other entity that creates IRIs for xAPI use or hosts metadata describing those IRIs.
The practice of attaching structured descriptive terms or identifiers to learning resources, events, competencies, or other entities.
A credential representing demonstrated achievement in a smaller unit of learning or competency than a traditional degree or major qualification.
Learning delivered in small, focused units that are often self-paced, flexible, and designed for use near the moment of need.
A benchmark representing the basic knowledge or skill expected in a learning domain, such as reading or mathematics, at a given age or grade.
A continuum of immersive technologies that includes virtual reality and augmented reality, combining physical and digital experience to varying degrees.
Learning delivered or supported through mobile devices, often enabling context-aware, pervasive access to learning at the point of need.
The use of abstract or computational representations to explore how systems, scenarios, behaviors, or designs may operate under different conditions.
The processes that influence whether a learner initiates, directs, persists in, and values an activity.
Remote learning delivered through a combination of channels such as radio, television, mobile devices, and online platforms in order to reach learners with different levels of access.
An approach that brings together actors inside and outside the education system to participate in the design and implementation of education technology programs and policies.
Learning that uses more than one mode of information presentation, such as combining words, narration, graphics, animation, or other media within an instructional environment.
In the xAPI Profile Server model, the RDF graph used to store a particular Profile version under that version’s URI so the version can be queried directly.
A nationally established quantitative reference point used to translate global SDG 4 ambitions into context-sensitive targets for monitoring progress, accountability, planning, and policy dialogue.
A connected community of researchers, practitioners, and other participants that shares expertise, builds relationships, supports collaboration, and extends work across projects and disciplines.
A subtle design intervention intended to steer behavior toward a desired choice without removing options or requiring direct command.
Learning that occurs through observing the behavior, strategies, actions, or consequences experienced by others.
A mode of online or remote learning that can be described along dimensions such as synchronous versus asynchronous participation and instructor-facilitated versus resource-facilitated activity.
Learning resources made openly available for people to use, share, and often adapt under open licensing terms.

en.prefLabel: Open standards and architecture for interoperability
en.definition: The use of open technology standards and interoperable architecture so data can be shared across applications, systems, and organizations in efficient, appropriate, and safe ways.
The degree to which a proposed learning solution can be implemented, supported, governed, maintained, and sustained in its real operating environment.
The practice of setting direction, aligning people and resources, shaping culture, and enabling an organization to achieve shared goals.
The process of validating a series of Statements that share a registration, and when applicable a subregistration, to determine whether they follow a specified Profile Pattern.
An animated or computational character designed to act as a tutor, peer, guide, or other social presence within an instructional technology.
The theory and practice of teaching, including choices about methods, sequencing, interaction, explanation, practice, and support.
An xAPI response object that combines known identifying information about an Agent into arrays of values, providing a person-centric view of Agent data while remaining distinct from an Agent persona.
A research-informed representation of a user type used to help teams reason about goals, behaviors, contexts, and needs.
The adjustment of learning content, sequencing, support, interface, or goals to characteristics or needs associated with an individual learner.
Learning designed around the needs of an individual student and intended to provide appropriate learning opportunities across school and home contexts.
Knowledge and professional judgment developed through direct practice, including practical understanding of learners, settings, workflows, constraints, and implementation.
The use of statistical or machine-learning models to estimate future outcomes, probabilities, or behaviors from available data.
Knowledge and understanding a learner already has and uses as a reference point for making sense of new ideas.
An approach in which privacy protections are incorporated into a system's architecture and development process from the beginning rather than added after deployment.
The use of interface cues, defaults, explanations, or other design interventions to help users make more informed privacy choices.
The contextual setting in which a learning challenge exists, including the conditions, constraints, learners, stakeholders, systems, and uncertainties that shape possible solutions.
Knowledge of how to carry out a procedure, perform a task, or solve a problem.
A pattern of beliefs and attitudes that supports effort, persistence, strategy use, and engagement with learning challenges.
A person or group writing an xAPI Profile.
A centralized service for finding, browsing, querying, storing, and managing xAPI Profiles, vocabulary concepts, and related Profile metadata.
A person or machine that verifies whether a particular set of xAPI data follows the rules in a Profile.
An xAPI Profile as it exists at a particular point in time, with version history that can be retained and queried independently.

Conformance in which Statements follow the matching Statement Templates and Patterns described by a Profile version, with the Profile version identified as a category context activity when authored by a conformant Learning Record Provider.
The discipline of planning, coordinating, monitoring, and controlling work so that objectives can be achieved within constraints such as scope, time, cost, quality, and resources.
An early representation of a proposed solution used to explore ideas, test assumptions, gather feedback, or reduce uncertainty.
The practice of creating low-cost or limited versions of a solution quickly so they can be tested and revised.
Documentation used during design to externalize decisions, reasoning, and context so practitioners can reflect on and revisit the work as it develops.
An identifier for an instance of an Actor experiencing a particular Activity.
Learning in which learners and teachers may be separated by time and/or location and interact through computers or telecommunications technologies.
The assignment of people, budget, time, technology, and other resources to work or objectives.
A semantic data model that represents information as subject–predicate–object relationships, allowing identifiers and relationships to be combined across datasets.
Learning in which structured resources, tools, content, or automated systems provide much of the support that guides learner activity.
The design, use, and governance of AI systems with attention to evidence, safety, privacy, fairness, transparency, accountability, and human consequences.
A web interface style in which software exchanges resources and data through standard HTTP methods and network conventions.
The optional xAPI Statement component used to represent a measured outcome, including values such as score, success, completion, response, duration, and extensions.
A learning strategy in which learners actively recall information from memory rather than only re-reading or reviewing it.
The systematic publication, examination, and tracking of education information against plans, indicators, targets, and benchmarks to support transparency, accountability, and continuous improvement.

en.prefLabel: Safe and responsible use of AI
en.definition: The use of AI in ways that apply ethical rules, protect privacy and intellectual property, follow applicable legal requirements, mitigate bias and harm, and preserve human responsibility.
A framework describing four levels of technology use in learning: substitution, augmentation, modification, and redefinition.
Temporary support that helps learners perform tasks or understand ideas that would otherwise be beyond their current independent capability.
The ability of a learning solution, system, or process to handle growth in users, data, complexity, scope, or demand without unacceptable degradation.
Reports and forms provided to higher-level authorities as part of regulatory accountability requirements.
An agile framework that organizes work into short cycles with defined roles, planning, review, and adaptation.
The protection of systems and data against unauthorized access, alteration, disclosure, disruption, or destruction.
A person’s belief in their capability to perform a particular task or succeed in a particular context.
A learner’s ongoing observation of their own time, tasks, understanding, stress, progress, and learning behavior in order to decide when adjustments are needed.
Learning in which individuals plan, monitor, evaluate, and adjust their goals, strategies, effort, and behavior.
The social and cognitive process of interpreting complex or ambiguous information by connecting observations, experiences, narratives, and shared context.
A hardware or software mechanism that detects an event, state, signal, or condition and makes it available for recording or processing.
A machine-readable way to define and exchange competencies using the IEEE 1484.20.3 standard.
Memory that temporarily holds a limited amount of information for immediate use.
An xAPI Statement that includes a JSON Web Signature as an Attachment so that the authenticity and integrity of the original Statement serialization can be verified.
A W3C vocabulary for representing concepts and semantic relationships among them in machine-readable form.
A representation of a real or imagined environment, process, or system used for practice, experimentation, analysis, or testing.
A view of learning that emphasizes the role of interaction, language, culture, and shared activity in the construction of knowledge.
The use of training, exercises, and organizational learning to strengthen people's ability to recognize, prevent, contain, and respond to security threats.
Learning that develops through interaction with other people and communities, including observation, conversation, collaboration, participation, and shared sensemaking.
The responsibility to consider and act on the wider effects of AI on human welfare, inclusion, social justice, civic life, and the environment.
The systematic design, development, testing, deployment, maintenance, and evolution of software systems.
A factor cited as informing or justifying a design decision, such as data, research, experience, stakeholder requirements, technology, or context.
A learning strategy that revisits information over increasing or strategically chosen intervals rather than concentrating practice in one session.
A query language for RDF data that allows semantic datasets to be searched by their entities, properties, and relationships.
The practice of involving people who are affected by, responsible for, or able to influence a learning challenge or solution.
A goal, requirement, recommendation, or idea expressed by a stakeholder that influences a design decision.
The degree to which a system, implementation, or dataset conforms to the requirements of a published standard or specification.
The xAPI resource at /activities/state used to store and retrieve arbitrary state documents associated with an Agent or Identified Group in an Activity, optionally tied to a registration.

The xAPI principle that key semantic parts of a Statement are not changed after the Statement has been stored. The standard identifies specific properties that are immutable and others that may differ without changing the Statement’s essential meaning.
An xAPI Object that refers to another Statement by UUID and uses the objectType StatementRef.
The LRS resource at /statements used to store and retrieve xAPI Statements, including single Statements, batches, and filtered Statement results.
The response structure returned when an LRS query retrieves multiple Statements, containing the returned Statements and, when more results are available, a link for retrieving the next set.
A set of rules describing one way Statements that use particular Concepts may be structured when following a Profile.
A restriction in a Statement Template that identifies one or more Statement locations with JSONPath and constrains the values or presence allowed there.
The process of validating a Statement against a Profile’s Statement Templates to determine which templates match and whether the matching templates’ rules are satisfied.

A structured process for defining a desired future state, understanding current conditions, identifying priorities and constraints, and organizing actions and resources to move an organization toward its goals.
A continuous flow of activity- and event-based data generated as learners interact with digital systems, content, people, and environments.
A person with deep knowledge or performance expertise in the domain a learning solution addresses.
An xAPI Profiles extension used to distinguish multiple Patterns being followed within the same xAPI registration.

An xAPI Statement-like Object embedded inside another Statement. It contains an Actor, Verb, and Object and may include Result, Context, Timestamp, and Attachments, but cannot itself contain another SubStatement.
Assessment used to judge or document learning at the end of a defined period, course, or instructional sequence.
Education-relevant data collected through instruments such as household surveys, labour-force surveys, and population censuses, often providing information not captured in administrative systems.
Learning activity that occurs in real time, with participants engaging at the same time and often together in a shared physical or virtual setting.
A larger capability formed by multiple independent or semi-independent systems whose interactions create behaviors and outcomes at the enterprise level.
An approach to understanding problems by examining components, relationships, feedback, boundaries, and behavior across the whole system.
A method for identifying the actions, knowledge, decisions, conditions, tools, and performance requirements involved in completing a task.
The organized methods and processes used to facilitate learning and develop knowledge or skills through instruction, practice, guidance, and training.
Fields of study focused on occupational, technical, professional, and vocational knowledge and skills, including preparation for specific skilled occupations and professions.
A feature or capability of a technology that can be used strategically to support a learning design decision.
A limit of a technology or platform that restricts or bounds a design decision.
Evaluation that examines whether a solution changes learning, retention, transfer, performance, or other intended outcomes rather than only usability or satisfaction.
The full lifecycle cost of acquiring, integrating, operating, supporting, changing, and retiring a technology or system.
A standards-based approach to interoperable learning ecosystems that connects learning activity data, learner information, competencies, analytics, and other services across systems.
AI used in education that is reliable and safe, robust against manipulation, protective of privacy and sensitive data, and appropriate to learners’ ages and pedagogical needs.
Learning understood as occurring across many places, times, devices, and contexts, including formal, nonformal, informal, workplace, and everyday settings.
Evaluation in which representative users attempt tasks so a team can observe where an interface or experience succeeds, confuses, or creates friction.
Direct evaluation of a design or system with intended or representative users.
A design approach that begins with the needs, contexts, and experiences of end users and stakeholders and uses that understanding to shape flexible, inclusive solutions.
The ability for users to adapt how a learning technology behaves or is configured to fit their needs, experience, context, or desired level of support.
A privacy approach in which a system models an individual learner's privacy concerns and adapts privacy information, recommendations, or decision support to that user.
A lean method for visualizing the flow of work and identifying delays, handoffs, bottlenecks, and activities that do not add value.
A condition in which earlier technology choices constrain future decisions because systems, data, or services are difficult to move, replace, or integrate.
The xAPI element that identifies the action performed by an Actor. A Verb is identified by an IRI, while a language map can provide human-readable display text.
A record of learning, skills, achievements, or employment information designed so claims can be checked or validated by other parties.
A multi-person learning environment created in software and supported by networked computer-mediated communication rather than a shared physical room.
A persistent networked environment in which people are represented through avatars and interact with one another and the environment through computers.
A previously issued xAPI Statement that has been marked invalid through a separate voiding Statement that targets it by Statement Reference.
An approach in which multiple government ministries and authorities coordinate around a shared policy or implementation challenge rather than treating it as the responsibility of a single agency.
An approach to development that treats cognitive, social, emotional, and physical capabilities as interconnected parts of learning across a person's life.
A step-by-step demonstration of how to perform a task or solve a problem, used to show learners how a complete solution is constructed.
The limited-capacity memory system in which information is consciously processed before it may be encoded into long-term memory.
The HTTP header used in xAPI requests and responses to declare the xAPI version being used.
An xAPI representation of an individual Actor, identified through one of the identity properties defined by the standard and optionally accompanied by a name.
The Agent or Group represented in a Statement as asserting that the Statement is true. The LRS verifies or sets the authority based on authentication and trust relationships.
Any entity that interacts with xAPI services through requests, including Learning Record Providers, Learning Record Consumers, Learning Record Stores, or other systems.
The xAPI use of HTTP entity tags and conditional request headers to prevent State, Agent Profile, or Activity Profile updates and deletes from being based on stale data.

Document data stored through the xAPI State, Agent Profile, or Activity Profile Resources. These resources store state or profile information in a generic document form scoped to an Activity, Agent or Identified Group, and, for State, optionally a registration.
A duration value used in xAPI to represent elapsed time for an experience or result, formatted according to the ISO 8601 duration rules referenced by the standard.

A custom property expressed in an xAPI extensions map using an IRI as the key and any JSON value or structure as the value. Extensions can appear in Activity Definitions, Statement Context, or Statement Result.
An xAPI Actor representation for a collection of Agents. A Group can be identified by its own identifier or anonymous and represented by its members.
A description of groups of xAPI Statements that match particular Statement Templates and are arranged according to specified ordering structures.
A set of one or more identity representations that uniquely describes an Actor in a particular context. The standard distinguishes personas from the broader real-world person.
The time at which the event described by a Statement occurred, represented using the timestamp rules defined by xAPI, including ISO 8601 and RFC 3339 formatting.
A principle describing how performance can vary with arousal or stress, often represented as an inverted-U relationship whose optimal level depends on task characteristics.
